purpose: Machine-readable inventory of every trajectory-related source examined in Phase 5A, with its access, precision, licensing and the strongest evidence level it can honestly support. The prose inventory in docs/launch-trajectory-sources.md carries the same ids and the tests check that the two agree.
levels: Evidence levels 1-5 are defined in src/launches/launch-trajectory.mjs and docs/launch-trajectory-feasibility.md.

sources.citation: SpaceX press kit, quoted here through the Oberg 2018 review draft
sources.coverage: Falcon 9, Falcon Heavy and Starship, one document per mission
sources.limitations: Pages are script-rendered with no API. The 2018 SAOCOM 1A press kit URL now returns 404 and survives only in the Internet Archive, so a pipeline cannot rely on the source staying available. Timelines give altitudes for a few events and no downrange, which cannot be turned into a bearing.
sources.name: SpaceX mission pages and press kits
sources.spatial_precision: none: no ground position is published
sources.update_frequency: per mission; historical URLs are withdrawn

sources.citation: SpaceX launch webcasts and the third-party transcriptions derived from them
sources.coverage: every mission since 2010, in archived video
sources.limitations: The source of the public reconstructions, read by a human or transcribed by a third party. The telemetry graphics have changed repeatedly and are not published as data, so a pipeline built on them depends on somebody else's transcription.
sources.name: SpaceX launch webcasts

sources.citation: 14 CFR part 420, Appendix B, Method for Defining a Flight Corridor
sources.coverage: the licensing framework for every us commercial launch
sources.limitations: Appendix B tells an applicant how to build a flight corridor from a one-second nominal trajectory and local wind statistics, and lists the vehicle parameters a trajectory generator must model. The trajectory itself belongs to the operator and is not published with the licence, so the regulation proves that precise trajectories exist without making any of them available.
sources.name: 14 CFR part 420 and its appendices, including Appendix B to part 420
sources.spatial_precision: not applicable: a method, not data
sources.temporal_precision: the regulation requires a nominal trajectory sampled at one second or finer

sources.citation: FAA Office of Commercial Space Transportation licensing documents
sources.coverage: site and vehicle programmes, not individual flights
sources.limitations: Maps sit inside PDFs as figures, so polygons have to be digitised by hand. A corridor bounds where debris may land under failure assumptions; it is not the vehicle's path.
sources.name: FAA licence orders, environmental assessments and environmental impact statements
sources.spatial_precision: hazard areas and corridors, kilometres to tens of kilometres

sources.citation: FAA TFR service, layer TFR:V_TFR_LOC, fetched 2026-10-16
sources.coverage: every active TFR, including space-operation TFRs
sources.limitations: Verified working: a GetFeature request returned GeoJSON with a polygon, a NOTAM key, a title and a legal category, with no key and no registration. It carries no launch-specific geometry beyond the surface area, and no altitude profile or time-resolved position.
sources.name: FAA temporary flight restriction geoserver (OGC WFS)

sources.limitations: The web interface refuses automated access and the machine-to-machine feed needs an account. Coordinates arrive inside free text, so a parser is required and it will break when the prose changes.
sources.name: FAA notices to air missions (NOTAM search and the SWIM feed)

sources.citation: USCG Navigation Center, local notices to mariners
sources.coverage: us coastal waters, weekly by district
sources.limitations: Distributed as weekly PDFs. Requests from this environment were refused by the host, so automated retrieval was not demonstrated and is not assumed. Launch hazard areas appear as prose and diagrams with no machine-readable polygon.
sources.name: US Coast Guard local notices to mariners and broadcast notices
sources.spatial_precision: named hazard areas with coordinates in the text

sources.limitations: Structured access sits behind a registered key; warnings are prose about a downrange area and do not resolve the ascent.
sources.name: NGA maritime safety information (NAVAREA warnings)

sources.citation: Telemetry-Data repository, Unlicense, reduced by scripts/build-trajectory-fixtures.mjs
sources.coverage: about sixty Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy flights, mainly 2016 to 2019; no Starship and nothing recent
sources.limitations: The best public time series that exists: altitude, speed, downrange and event times at one-second spacing, released to the public domain. It is a third-party transcription of a webcast graphic, not operator telemetry. This phase measured its terminal state against the achieved orbits in GCAT and found the altitude series and the speed series disagree with the orbit in different ways for different flights, so absolute values cannot be trusted without an independent anchor.
sources.name: Webcast telemetry transcriptions (shahar603/Telemetry-Data)
sources.spatial_precision: none: altitude and downrange only, no position
sources.temporal_precision: one second, event times to the second

sources.citation: McDowell, J., 2020, General Catalog of Artificial Space Objects, CC-BY-4.0
sources.coverage: every orbital launch, with achieved orbits per payload
sources.limitations: Gives the pad, the time and the achieved orbit, which is what is needed to validate or anchor a reconstruction, and nothing about the ascent itself. Attribution is required.
sources.name: General Catalog of Artificial Space Objects (J. McDowell)
sources.temporal_precision: to the second for some launches, a day for others

sources.citation: CelesTrak, with Space-Track for registration-gated access
sources.coverage: objects that reached orbit, including spent upper stages
sources.limitations: The first useful element set appears after insertion, so it anchors the end state of an ascent rather than the ascent. CelesTrak is already the project's satellite source; only its role as an anchor is new here.
sources.name: CelesTrak and Space-Track element sets for launch-related objects

sources.citation: Flight Club commercial usage page and API documentation, read 2026-10-16
sources.coverage: most orbital launches, curated per flight
sources.limitations: Publishes an OpenAPI-documented developer interface and sells commercial licences shaped by volume, redistribution and branding, so its data cannot be redistributed in a public product without a negotiated agreement. The modelling method and its error budget are not published, which is itself a scientific limitation.
sources.name: Flight Club
sources.spatial_precision: claimed high fidelity, method not published
sources.temporal_precision: sub-second in the published mission profiles

sources.limitations: An engine, not a data source. A credible Falcon 9 or Starship simulation needs mass, thrust and specific impulse against time, stage dimensions, aerodynamic coefficients and wind profiles. Appendix B lists exactly those parameters as applicant-supplied, and no operator publishes them, so a simulation built without them would be an invented trajectory dressed as a model output.
sources.name: RocketPy and similar open-source ascent simulators
sources.spatial_precision: set by the assumed vehicle model

sources.citation: Oberg, J., Analysis of Observations of SpaceX Falcon-9 Launch October 7, 2018, REVIEW DRAFT 2, 8 December 2018
sources.limitations: A 122-page review draft, explicitly incomplete, that pairs observer coordinates with video-derived bearings and includes an altitude-versus-elevation method using the law of sines. It is the best independent ground truth found for a single flight, and its derived bearings carry the several-degree uncertainty the author states.
sources.name: Independent observation analyses, including Oberg's review draft on the 2018 SAOCOM 1A ascent
sources.spatial_precision: observer coordinates in a few cases, tens of kilometres in others

sources.citation: NASA APOD 2017 December 24, image credit Craig Bobchin
sources.limitations: Published photographs rarely state a bearing, an exposure orientation or an exact location, so they can corroborate that something was seen and cannot measure where it was. Image rights rest with the photographers.
sources.name: NASA Astronomy Picture of the Day and press imagery
